articles.title: Why Are Teenagers So Tired in the Morning?
articles.dek: At night you are wide awake, but in the morning you can't get up. Why?
paras: It is seven o'clock on a Monday morning. Your alarm is ringing, but you can't open your eyes. Then at eleven o'clock at night, you are not tired at all. Does this happen to you? It happens to a lot of teenagers. But why? Let's find out step by step.

First, your body has got a kind of clock inside it. This body clock tells you when to sleep and when to wake up. In the evening, when it gets dark, your brain makes a special chemical. Its name is melatonin. It helps you feel sleepy.

Young children usually make melatonin early in the evening. So they often fall asleep at seven or eight o'clock. But when you become a teenager, your body clock changes. Your body starts to make melatonin later in the day. You also start to feel tired more slowly. That is why many teenagers don't feel sleepy until eleven o'clock or midnight. They are not lazy. Their bodies are working in a different way.

But school doesn't start later for teenagers! Most students have to get up early in the morning. Doctors say that teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep every night. Children from six to twelve need even more: nine to twelve hours. So if you go to bed at midnight and get up at seven, you don't get enough sleep.

Is sleep really so important? Yes, it is! At night, your brain is very busy. It helps you remember the new things from the day. After a good night's sleep, you can think more clearly in class. It is also easier to learn a new song or a new sport.

So what can you do? Put your phone away about half an hour before bed. The light from screens can stop your body from making melatonin. Try to go to bed at the same time on school nights. And at the weekend, enjoy a little more sleep on Saturday and Sunday mornings!

articles.title: Notices at Riverside Library
articles.dek: Where is the study room? Where do your books go? Read the signs and find out.
paras: Riverside Library is a big library in the middle of a busy town. It has got books, computers and a small café. Leo Kim is fourteen, and he goes there every Saturday. Today he is reading the notices and messages around the building. Here are some of them.

SIGN by the front door: Welcome to Riverside Library! Children's books are on the ground floor, next to the café. Books for teenagers and adults are upstairs on the first floor. The study room is at the end of the corridor, opposite the lift. Please go up the stairs or take the lift.

NOTICE above the return box: Are you returning a book? Put it into this box, please. Don't leave books on the floor in front of the box. After 6 p.m., push your books through the hole in the wall outside. We open again at 9 a.m.

NOTICE in the computer room: Computers are free for library members. Please book a computer at the desk behind you. You can use it for one hour. Don't put drinks on the tables near the computers! The printer is between the two windows.

Text message from Leo to his friend Maya: Hi Maya, I'm at the library. I'm sitting at a table near the window, under the big clock. I've found three good books for our history project. Come in through the side door. The front door is closed today. Leo

NOTE on the noticeboard: LOST! A blue pencil case with a cat on it. I think I left it under a chair in the study room on Thursday. If you find it, please give it to the woman at the front desk. Thank you! Amira

POSTER next to the lift: Story time for little children! Every Wednesday at 4 p.m. Walk past the café and go into the yellow room. Sit on the soft carpet and listen to a new story. Parents can wait outside the room.

articles.title: Clothes with a Story
articles.dek: Three teenagers tell us about their favourite clothes – and whose they were first.
paras: Have you got a piece of clothing with a special story? Maybe it was a present. Or maybe it was someone else's first. We asked three teenagers about their favourite clothes. Here are their answers.

Hana, 13: My favourite jumper isn't really mine. It's my brother's! Kenji is seventeen, and the jumper is too small for him now. It's dark green, and it has got a big yellow star on the front. Kenji says he wants it back one day. But I don't think so! I wear it every Sunday. Last week Mum asked, 'Whose jumper is this?' I said, 'It's mine now!'

Diego, 15: My favourite thing is a red football shirt. It was my grandfather's shirt fifty years ago. He played for a small team in his village in Mexico. The shirt is old, and there is a little hole in one sleeve. I never wear it for football. It hangs on the wall of my bedroom. My friends' shirts are new and shiny, but mine has a story.

Freya, 14: I love my grey trainers. My best friend Lily has got the same ones. One day after PE, we couldn't find our trainers. There were two grey pairs under the bench. 'Whose are these?' Lily asked. 'Are they yours or mine?' Then I saw a small blue heart on one shoe. I drew it there in the summer. So those trainers were mine, and the others were hers!
What about you? Is there something in your wardrobe with a story? Is it yours, or was it someone else's first? Write and tell us!

grammar.rule: Use my, your, his, her, our, their before a noun: my jumper. Use mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs with no noun after them: It's mine. Use 's for one person (my brother's) and s' for plural nouns (my friends'). Ask with whose.

examples.text: Last week Mum asked, 'Whose jumper is this?'
My friends' shirts are new and shiny, but mine has a story.

items.why: No noun after it, so we use hers.

items.q: ___ trainers are these? They are very dirty!
items.why: We ask about the owner with whose.

items.q: Yesterday I ___ my sister's coat because ___ was wet.
items.why: Past simple: wore; no noun after it, so mine.

items.q: The ___ clothes are in the big bag by the door.
items.why: children is plural but has no s, so we add 's.

items.q: Is this cap ___ ? – No, it isn't mine. It's ___ .
items.why: yours with no noun; Tom's for one person.

items.q: Last month my parents ___ a new wardrobe. ___ old one was too small.
items.why: Past simple: bought; their + noun (old one).

kps.fact: Hana wears her brother's green jumper because it is too small for him.
Diego's red football shirt was his grandfather's fifty years ago.
kps.q: Who wore the red shirt first?

kps.fact: Diego never wears the shirt. It hangs on his bedroom wall.
Freya and Lily have got the same grey trainers.
kps.q: What is the same about Freya and Lily?

kps.fact: A small blue heart showed which trainers were Freya's.
kps.q: How did Freya find her trainers?

summary.intro: Choose the three sentences that tell the main ideas of the text.
summary.model: Hana and Diego wear clothes that belonged to their family first. Freya and Lily have the same trainers, but a blue heart shows whose are whose.

options.t: Hana's favourite jumper was her brother's first.
Diego keeps his grandfather's old football shirt.
options.evidence: It was my grandfather's shirt fifty years ago.

options.t: Freya found her trainers because of a small blue heart.
options.evidence: Then I saw a small blue heart on one shoe.

options.t: Hana's jumper has got a yellow star on it.
options.why: True, but it is only a small detail.
options.evidence: It's dark green, and it has got a big yellow star on the front.

options.t: Freya bought her trainers in a big shop in town.
Diego wears the red shirt in every football match.
options.why: Wrong: he never wears it for football.
options.evidence: I never wear it for football.

Say who helped you and what happened.
